Stimulus:
Pedigree for Syndrome X (three generations):

Generation I:  I-1 (affected female) × I-2 (unaffected male)
Generation II: II-1 (affected male), II-2 (unaffected female), II-3 (affected female), II-4 (unaffected male), II-5 (unaffected male), II-6 (unaffected female)
Generation III: III-1 (unaffected), III-2 (affected), III-3 (unaffected), III-4 (unaffected)

Note: II-3 and II-4 are mated (III-1 through III-4 are their children). II-4 is a known carrier.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the pedigree, determine the most likely mode of inheritance of Syndrome X (autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, or X-linked recessive). Provide evidence from the pedigree to justify your answer. Then determine the genotypes of individuals I-1, I-2, II-3, and II-4.

Part B: Individual II-3 and individual II-4 (who is phenotypically unaffected but a known carrier) plan to have children.
Using a Punnett square or probability notation, determine the probability that their first child will be affected by Syndrome X.
Individual II-3 and II-4 have four children. Three are unaffected and one is affected. Perform a chi-square (χ²) analysis to determine whether these data are consistent with the expected ratio. Use a significance level of p = 0.05 and 1 degree of freedom (χ²_crit = 3.84).

Part C: A new genetic test reveals that the gene responsible for Syndrome X is located on chromosome 7, approximately 8 cM from a molecular marker called M1. In a test cross of an individual heterozygous at both loci (in coupling) with a doubly homozygous recessive individual, 200 offspring are produced.
Predict the number of offspring expected in each of the four phenotypic classes.
Explain why the linked loci produce offspring frequencies that differ from the 1:1:1:1 ratio expected if the loci were unlinked.

Part D: Explain how nondisjunction of chromosome 7 during meiosis II changes the chromosome number of the resulting gametes. Predict the chromosome number of a zygote formed when an abnormal gamete containing two copies of chromosome 7 is fertilized by a normal gamete.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Determines autosomal-recessive inheritance using pedigree evidence and assigns I-1=aa, I-2=Aa, II-3=aa, and II-4=Aa.
- Determines a 1/2 affected-child probability and completes a chi-square analysis of 3 unaffected and 1 affected child against the 1:1 expectation.
- Predicts linked-testcross offspring counts of 92, 92, 8, and 8 and explains why linkage causes departure from the unlinked 1:1:1:1 expectation.
- Explains that failure of sister chromatids to separate in meiosis II produces one gamete with two copies of chromosome 7 and one with none; fertilization of the disomic gamete by a normal gamete produces a trisomic zygote.

Stimulus:
DNA replication and gene expression are fundamental processes of the central dogma. Key facts:

• DNA replication is semiconservative: each daughter molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand
• Replication occurs 5'→3' on the new strand; the template is read 3'→5'
• RNA polymerase synthesizes mRNA using the template (antisense) strand
• The genetic code is read in triplet codons (non-overlapping)
• AUG = start codon (Met); UAA, UAG, UGA = stop codons

Partial codon table (relevant to part c):
AUC = Ile | GGA = Gly | UCC = Ser | AAG = Lys | UCG = Ser
AUG = Met | CCA = Pro | AGU = Ser | CUU = Leu
UAG = stop | UCA = Ser | GAC = Asp | GUC = Val

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The Meselson-Stahl experiment demonstrated that DNA replication is semiconservative. Describe the experimental design and results of the Meselson-Stahl experiment. Explain how the results support the semiconservative model rather than the conservative or dispersive models.

Part B: Describe the roles of the following enzymes during DNA replication in eukaryotes, and explain why each is necessary:
Helicase
DNA primase
DNA polymerase III (or the equivalent leading-strand polymerase)
DNA ligase

Part C: The template DNA strand for a gene has the following sequence:
5'-ATCGGATCCAAGTCG-3'
Write the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this template strand.
Using the genetic code table, determine the amino acid sequence encoded by the mRNA, beginning from the first codon. Identify which codon, if any, is a start codon or stop codon.
A point mutation changes the 8th base of the template strand from C to T. Determine whether this mutation is synonymous or nonsynonymous, and explain the consequence for the protein.

Part D: A researcher treats cells with a drug that specifically blocks the activity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Predict and explain the cellular consequences of this drug treatment for protein synthesis.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe the Meselson-Stahl experiment and explain how results support semiconservative replication.
- Describe the roles of helicase, DNA primase, DNA polymerase III, and DNA ligase in replication.
- Write the mRNA sequence; determine the amino acid sequence; analyze the point mutation.
- Predict and explain the consequences of blocking aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.

Stimulus:
Table 1: Mean beak depth (mm) of the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on Daphne Major Island, Galápagos

Year | Mean beak depth (mm) | Sample size | Notes
1976 |        9.42          |    642      | Pre-drought
1977 |        9.96          |    85       | During drought (severe dry season)
1978 |       10.07          |    388      | Post-drought recovery

Drought conditions (1976-1977): Small soft seeds became scarce first; large hard seeds remained available longer. Birds with larger, deeper beaks could crack large seeds that smaller-beaked birds could not process.

Survival: 85 of 642 birds survived the drought. Mean beak depth of survivors = 9.96 mm (significantly larger than pre-drought mean of 9.42 mm).

Table 2: Allele frequencies for a beak depth quantitative trait locus (simplified diploid model)
Allele D (associated with deeper beaks): frequency = 0.6
Allele d (associated with shallower beaks): frequency = 0.4

Observed genotype frequencies in 1976 population (N=642):
DD: 0.40 | Dd: 0.42 | dd: 0.18

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Analyze the beak depth data from Table 1. Using evidence from the data, describe the change in the finch population's beak depth between 1976 and 1978, and explain the mechanism of natural selection responsible for this change. Address: the source of variation, the selective agent, differential survival, and heritability.

Part B: Using the allele frequencies provided in Table 2, determine whether the medium ground finch population in 1976 was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the beak depth gene. Show all calculations. (Use p = frequency of allele D; q = frequency of allele d.)

Part C: A 1983 El Niño event brought heavy rainfall to the Galápagos, dramatically increasing the abundance of small soft seeds. By 1984, mean beak depth had shifted back toward smaller values.
Identify the type of natural selection acting on beak depth after the 1983 El Niño, and explain why small beak depth was favored.
Explain why this shift in beak depth does NOT represent Lamarckian inheritance.

Part D: The large ground finch (Geospiza magnirostris) arrived on Daphne Major Island after 1982 and occupies a similar ecological niche to the medium ground finch. Explain the concept of competitive exclusion and predict what might happen to the medium ground finch population as a result of G. magnirostris's arrival. Describe ONE possible evolutionary outcome for the medium ground finch population that would allow coexistence.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Analyze beak depth data and explain the mechanism of natural selection — variation, selective agent, differential survival, heritability.
- Test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium using 1976 allele frequencies; show all calculations.
- Identify selection type after 1983 El Niño; explain why this is not Lamarckian.
- Explain competitive exclusion; predict outcome for medium ground finch; describe an evolutionary coexistence outcome.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: A student sets up the following experiment: potato (Solanum tuberosum) cylinders of equal mass are placed in sucrose solutions of varying concentrations for 24 hours. Mass change is recorded.
Using the data in Table 1, graph the percent mass change versus sucrose concentration (or describe the graph's decreasing trend and label the near-zero crossing between 0.3 M and 0.4 M).
Estimate the sucrose concentration at which the potato tissue is in osmotic equilibrium with the surrounding solution. Explain what this concentration tells you about the effective solute concentration of the potato tissue.
At the 0.2 M sucrose solution, predict and explain the direction of net water movement and the expected physical state of the potato cells.

Part B: Water potential determines the direction of water movement. A potato cell with solute potential of -7.0 bars is placed in an external pure-water solution for which water potential = 0 bars and pressure potential = 0 bars.
Define water potential and write the equation Psi = Psi_s + Psi_p, defining each term.
Calculate the pressure potential of the potato cell at equilibrium with the external pure-water solution. Explain what this value represents in the context of plant cell turgor.

Part C: Compare the response of a plant cell and an animal cell (e.g., a red blood cell) placed in each of the following solutions. Use appropriate terminology (plasmolysis, crenation, lysis, turgor, etc.):
A hypotonic solution
A hypertonic solution

Part D: Aquaporins are membrane protein channels that facilitate the movement of water across cell membranes. A researcher finds that certain plant cells in a drought-stressed leaf can reduce water loss by decreasing aquaporin expression.
Explain the mechanism by which aquaporins facilitate water movement without violating the passive nature of osmosis.
Predict the effect of aquaporin deletion on a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution, compared to a normal cell. Explain your prediction.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Estimates osmotic equilibrium at about 0.35 M sucrose and explains that this estimates the potato tissue effective solute concentration.
- Graphs or accurately describes the decreasing relationship between sucrose concentration and percent mass change, including the near-zero crossing between 0.3 M and 0.4 M.
- Predicts water movement into the potato at 0.2 M and the resulting turgid state of the potato cells.
- Defines water potential and its components; calculates the potato cell pressure potential at equilibrium with the external pure-water solution.
- Compares plant-cell and animal-cell responses in both hypotonic and hypertonic solutions using correct terminology.
- Explain how aquaporins facilitate osmosis without violating passive transport; predict effect of aquaporin deletion in hypertonic solution.

Question:

Part A: Using the data in Table 1, describe how reaction rate changes as substrate concentration increases, and explain why the rate reaches a maximum (saturates) at high substrate concentration even though more substrate is available.

Part B: Table 2 shows the same enzyme's activity in the presence of Inhibitor A and Inhibitor B, each tested across a range of substrate concentrations. Part C: Some enzymes are regulated by allosteric inhibitors that are end products of the metabolic pathway the enzyme participates in. Explain how this represents allosteric regulation. Part D: Temperature affects enzyme activity in a characteristic bell-shaped curve.
Explain why enzyme activity increases from 0°C to the temperature optimum.
Explain why enzyme activity decreases sharply above the temperature optimum, connecting your answer to denaturation.

Stimulus:
The endomembrane system consists of the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, and plasma membrane. The nuclear envelope is directly continuous with the ER. Most other compartments are functionally connected by vesicular transport.

Golgi apparatus: proteins are modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing), sorted, and packaged. The cis face receives vesicles from the ER; the trans face sends vesicles toward their destinations.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: A pancreatic acinar cell synthesizes and secretes the digestive enzyme trypsinogen. Trace the complete pathway of a trypsinogen molecule from its synthesis to its secretion from the cell. Name each organelle or cellular structure involved and describe what happens to the protein at each step.

Part B: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) has functions distinct from the rough ER (RER). Describe THREE functions of the SER in a liver cell.

Part C: Lysosomes are membrane-bounded organelles containing digestive enzymes. Explain:
How the cell ensures its own digestive enzymes end up inside lysosomes rather than being secreted from the cell.
Why lysosomal enzymes do not destroy the lysosome's own membrane.
What happens when a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome.

Part D: A researcher treats cells with a drug that blocks vesicle budding from the Golgi apparatus. Predict and explain the effect of this treatment on: (i) secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein; (ii) delivery of digestive enzymes to lysosomes; (iii) the size and appearance of the ER in treated cells.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Trace the trypsinogen pathway through the named organelles (ribosome/RER -> Golgi -> secretory vesicle -> plasma membrane) and describe what happens at each step.
- Describe three SER functions (e.g. lipid synthesis, detoxification, calcium storage).
- Explain lysosomal enzyme targeting, why lysosomal enzymes do not digest the lysosome membrane, and what happens when a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome.
- Predict effects of blocking Golgi vesicle budding on secretion, lysosomal enzyme delivery, and ER appearance.

Stimulus:
Mitochondrial structure:
• Outer membrane: permeable to small molecules (porins)
• Intermembrane space: H⁺ accumulates here during electron transport
• Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae; contains electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase; impermeable to ions
• Matrix: contains Krebs cycle enzymes, mtDNA, mitochondrial ribosomes

The electron transport chain complexes in the inner membrane pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space as electrons pass through them; ATP synthase uses the resulting H⁺ gradient to synthesize ATP. Note: when the H⁺ gradient cannot be relieved by ATP synthase (e.g. if ATP synthase is blocked), electron flow through the chain and O₂ consumption also slow, because the chain works against the built-up gradient.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
Describe TWO OR THREE specific lines of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.

Part B: Describe the role of the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis. In your answer, explain: (i) the source of the proton gradient; (ii) how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase; and (iii) the general role of the electron transport chain complexes (supplied in the stimulus) in building that gradient.

Part C: A researcher adds the following compounds to isolated mitochondria respiring aerobically. For each compound, predict whether O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis will increase, decrease, or be unaffected, and explain your reasoning:
Rotenone (inhibits Complex I electron transfer)
Oligomycin (blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase)
Dinitrophenol / DNP (uncoupler — makes the inner membrane permeable to H⁺)

Part D: Heart muscle cells have unusually high numbers of mitochondria. Explain the functional reason for this, and describe the specific structural feature of mitochondria that maximizes ATP output.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe two or three lines of evidence for endosymbiosis (double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission).
- Explain (i) proton gradient source, (ii) how it drives ATP synthase, (iii) the general role of ETC complexes in building the gradient -- score (i)/(ii)/(iii) separately.
- Predict rotenone (decreases both), oligomycin (ATP synthesis decreases; O2 consumption also decreases per the stimulus note on coupled electron flow, or unaffected with sound reasoning accepted), and DNP (O2 consumption increases, ATP synthesis decreases) with reasoning for each.
- Explain why heart cells need many mitochondria and describe cristae as the structural feature that maximizes ATP output.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Describe, in general terms, how a glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is broken down through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle, and identify at which of these stages CO₂ is released.

Part B: For one molecule of glucose completely oxidized through aerobic respiration, explain which stages produce NADH and FADH₂, and explain how these electron carriers are used in the electron transport chain to ultimately produce ATP.

Part C: The actual ATP yield from one glucose molecule is lower than the theoretical maximum. Explain why, describing at least TWO general reasons the process is not perfectly efficient.

Part D: A cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Using the data in Table 1, which shows glucose consumption rates, explain why glucose consumption increases dramatically under anaerobic conditions. Your answer should connect the cell's ATP needs, the lower ATP yield of fermentation compared to aerobic respiration, and the need to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe glucose breakdown through the three stages in general terms and identify CO2-releasing steps.
- Identify which stages produce NADH/FADH2 and explain their general role feeding the ETC.
- Explain at least two general reasons actual ATP yield is lower than theoretical maximum.
- Explain increased anaerobic glucose consumption via ATP needs, fermentation's lower yield, and NAD+ regeneration.

Question:

Part A: Compare alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation, and explain the metabolic purpose both pathways share.

Part B: A claim states that fermentation directly produces ATP from the reactions shown in the stimulus. Evaluate this claim: identify which step, if any, produces ATP directly, and clarify where most of a cell's ATP actually comes from when oxygen is available.

Part C: Using Table 1, explain the CO₂ production values under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, explain why the anaerobic rate is higher, and predict the CO₂ production rate for the aerobic + cyanide condition, given that cyanide blocks the electron transport chain.

Part D: A common claim is that lactic acid directly causes the burning sensation in fatigued muscles. Evaluate this claim and explain what most directly causes muscle fatigue during intense anaerobic exercise.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation pathways and explain the metabolic purpose they share.
- Evaluate the claim that fermentation directly produces ATP; clarify which step produces ATP.
- Explain CO₂ under both conditions; explain higher anaerobic rate; predict cyanide effect.

Stimulus:
Insulin signaling pathway:
• Insulin binds → receptor α-subunits change conformation
• β-subunit cytoplasmic tails auto-phosphorylate tyrosines (kinase activation)
• IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) binds and is phosphorylated by receptor
• PI3K recruited → phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3
• PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt → PDK1 phosphorylates/activates Akt
• Active Akt phosphorylates downstream targets:
  – Phosphorylates AS160 → GLUT4 vesicle fusion with plasma membrane
  – Phosphorylates and inhibits GSK-3 → activates glycogen synthase
  – Activates mTOR → promotes protein synthesis
  – Phosphorylates and inactivates FOXO transcription factors

GPCR comparison:
• β-adrenergic receptor + epinephrine → Gα-GTP → adenylyl cyclase activated
• cAMP produced → PKA activated → multiple downstream phosphorylations

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Using the information provided, describe the mechanism by which insulin binding triggers GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane. Trace the signaling pathway from insulin binding at the receptor through to glucose uptake.

Part B: Compare the insulin/receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathway to the epinephrine/G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) pathway described. For each pathway, identify: the receptor type and location, the primary second messenger or amplification step, and one physiological effect.

Part C: Suppose a mutation causes the insulin receptor to be constitutively (continuously) active, even in the absence of insulin. Predict THREE consequences of this mutation for the cell, addressing metabolic effects, cell proliferation, and gene expression.

Part D: Several distinct mutations can produce excessive, insulin-independent growth signaling in cancer cells. For EACH of the following, explain how the described change leads to chronic activation of a growth-signaling pathway:
(i) Overexpression of the HER2 receptor
(ii) A Ras protein locked in its GTP-bound form
(iii) Loss-of-function mutation in the PTEN gene

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe insulin → RTK → IRS-1 → PI3K → Akt → GLUT4 pathway in sequence.
- Compare RTK (insulin) and GPCR (epinephrine) pathways on receptor type, second messenger, and physiological effect.
- Predict three consequences of constitutively active insulin receptor.
- Explain how HER2 overexpression, Ras-GTP lock, and PTEN loss each contribute to cancer.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The pedigree in Figure 1 shows the inheritance of a trait across three generations. Affected individuals are shaded. Determine the most likely mode of inheritance and justify your answer by identifying at least TWO pedigree observations that support your conclusion. Assign genotypes to individuals I-1, I-2, II-3 (an affected male), and II-4 (an unaffected female who has an affected son). Calculate the probability that a child of II-4 and II-3 will be an affected female.

Part B: Males with X-linked recessive conditions are affected at a much higher frequency than females. Explain the molecular and genetic basis for this sex difference, using hemizygosity in your explanation.

Part C: Explain X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) in female mammals. Describe when X-inactivation occurs in development and how the choice of which X is inactivated is made. Explain why the patches of orange and black fur are large rather than a uniform blended color. Predict the coat color pattern of a female cat that is homozygous for the orange allele.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Eukaryotic gene expression requires the coordinated action of transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and chromatin remodeling. Describe the sequence of events that leads to the assembly of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) at a eukaryotic promoter and name TWO general transcription factors and their roles. Explain how an enhancer element located 10,000 base pairs upstream of a gene can stimulate transcription at the gene's promoter, including the role of activator proteins and Mediator.

Part B: Chromatin structure regulates access to DNA. Using Figure 1 (which shows the same gene in euchromatin vs. heterochromatin states): Describe the structural difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin at the level of histone modification. Explain how histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) have opposite effects on transcription, including the mechanism by which acetylation opens chromatin. A researcher adds trichostatin A (an HDAC inhibitor) to cells. Predict and explain the effect on global gene expression.

Part C: Experiment: The researcher fuses the DNA-binding domain of a transcription factor to different activation domains and measures target gene expression. Results are shown in Table 1. What does the DNA-binding domain alone demonstrate about gene activation? What do the activation domain results reveal about how transcription is activated? The researcher finds that activation domain 3 interacts physically with the Mediator complex. Explain how this interaction could lead to increased transcription.

Part D: Explain how the following two mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression in a multicellular organism that has one genome but hundreds of distinct cell types: Combinatorial control by transcription factors and epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states.

Scoring criteria (what a complete answer must do; use these to judge the cognitive task, ignore any specific answer values):
- Describe PIC assembly at eukaryotic promoter naming two GTFs; explain enhancer-Mediator mechanism.
- Describe euchromatin/heterochromatin histone modifications; HAT/HDAC mechanisms; predict HDAC inhibitor effect.
- Interpret domain fusion experiment data; explain Mediator interaction mechanism.
- Explain cell-type-specific expression via combinatorial TF control and epigenetic inheritance.

Question:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies due to chance events. Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs mechanistically from natural selection as a cause of reduced genetic diversity. A cheetah population experienced a severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago. Today, all cheetahs are nearly genetically identical and can accept skin grafts from any other cheetah without rejection. Explain what this reveals about the level of genetic diversity in the cheetah population.
